summary: An April 1st humor RFC proposing a more compact way to write IPv6 addresses. It is a joke and not a serious proposal.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st RFC jokes about the length of written IPv6 addresses. It proposes encoding each address as 20 base-85 characters, with a detailed explanation delivered in a deadpan technical style.

what is the base 85 ipv6 address proposal

subtitle: An April 1st proposal to encode IPv6 addresses as fixed-length base-85 strings.

tldr.problem: IPv6 addresses are long to write in hexadecimal, even when zero groups are suppressed.
tldr.mechanism: This April 1st joke treats the 128-bit address as an integer and encodes it in base 85 using a selected set of printable ASCII characters.
tldr.outcome: The RFC proposes a fixed 20-character representation, but its deliberately unreadable result and implementation discussion are part of the joke.

today: RFC 1924 is listed as Informational and has no obsoleting or updating RFC in the unit metadata. It is an April 1st joke document.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Text Looks Long
sections.content:
RFC 1924 is an April 1st joke. It begins with the practical observation that an IPv6 address is 128 bits and can take many characters to write in conventional hexadecimal notation, even when zero groups are omitted.

The document proposes another text representation intended to encode every IPv6 address in a fixed length. The serious tone and detailed calculations set up the joke.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC starts with a real inconvenience: long addresses are hard to write. Its proposed solution is technically elaborate and intentionally comic.

sections.title: The Base-85 Representation
sections.content:
The proposed format treats the address as one 128-bit integer and writes it in base 85. The RFC chooses 85 printable characters, avoiding punctuation such as quotes, commas, periods, slashes, colons, brackets, and backslashes that could conflict with common syntax.

The RFC works through converting an address by repeated division and gives a sample string. It argues that 20 base-85 digits can represent every possible 128-bit address.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal turns the whole address into one large number and converts it to 20 characters. Its chosen characters avoid several punctuation marks used to format addresses.

sections.title: The Practical Joke
sections.content:
The memo presents the fixed-width format as a benefit and discusses the need for 128-bit integer arithmetic. It also jokes that the unfamiliar character string may make addresses harder for people and packet sniffers to recognize.

These claims belong to the RFC's parody of technical specifications. The document does not establish the proposed encoding as a standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal makes addresses shorter but much harder to recognize. The contrast between the detailed technical argument and the impractical result is the joke.
